part.text:
All 17 tests pass and `go vet` is clean. ## What I did Per `.docs/instructions.md`, this is a refactoring exercise: the original `markdown.go` was a single byte-at-a-time scanning loop with intertwined special cases (a `header` counter, `list` counter, `listOpened` flag, and an `he` "saw a header" flag, plus `strings.LastIndex` tricks to decide when to close a list). I rewrote it in `markdown.go` as a clean line-oriented parser: - **`Render`** splits the input into lines and classifies each one: - **Header** — 1–6 `#` chars followed by a space → `text` (a run of 7+ `#` is *not* a header, so `####### ...` stays paragraph text, matching the "h7 is a paragraph" test) - **List item** — line starting with `* ` → `
  • text
    • `, with consecutive items wrapped in one `
      ` - **Paragraph** — anything else, collected and flushed as a single `

      ` block (lines joined without separators, preserving the original's newline-discarding behavior) - **`parseHeader`** — small helper that detects a header line and returns its level and text. - **`applyEmphasis` / `replaceFirstPair`** — replaces the four chained `strings.Replace(..., 1)` calls with a single "first pair" helper, keeping the original semantics exactly: first `__` pair → ``, then first `_` pair → `` (the `_` pass runs on the string left by the `__` pass). Refactoring notes are captured in comments, as the spec suggests. Behavior is preserved for all tested inputs (I traced the original's output for each test case before rewriting); a couple of untested edge quirks of the old byte-scanner (e.g. `

    ` not being closed when a header follows a list, or an out-of-range panic on a lone `*` line) are handled more sensibly by the line-based design. `markdown_test.go` was not touched, and no new files were created.
